item.title: The Cultural Stock
item.author: pvolker@mdh-hability.com (Pvolker / Projeto Centauro)
item.description:
The Cultural Stock

My difficulty begins with the expression “genuinely human work.” What would, after all, a human work be that did not depend on everything that came before it? I do not write alone. No one writes alone. I write in a language I did not invent, with words I received, images I inherited, ways of narrating that were already in the world before me. I write from books read, conversations, films, music, memories, experiences, schools, cities, friends, losses, desires, and an entire culture that precedes me. The author is not the origin of the cultural stock. He is a point of passage.

Every culture has a stock: language, symbolic repertoire, historical memory, techniques, institutions, artistic media, ways of living together, knowledge, beliefs, instruments, and forms of expression. This stock delimits the space in which a society can create. To delimit is not to determine. The combinations can be nearly inexhaustible. But no one invents from nothing the elements with which they combine. An eighteenth-century European composer had at hand certain instruments, a harmonic tradition, a notation system, certain musical forms, and the soundscape of his time. An Ancient Greek sculptor could not make cinema. Not because he lacked talent, but because cinema was not yet part of the stock of possibilities of his culture.

All creation is an operation upon antecedents. It can combine, invert, condense, expand, displace, transform, negate. Sometimes it reorganizes what came before so profoundly that it expands the cultural stock itself: it introduces a new technique, a language, a form of perception. But even in that case it did not arise “ex nihilo.” It transformed something that already existed. For humans there will never be the “ex nihilo,” simply because, for any human, at birth, existence is given “ab omni” — already with everything. To be human is to be born into a chain that is already underway.

It is to receive a culture that does not belong to us individually and to return to it new configurations. The subject of the stock is not the isolated author. It is humanity in history. That is why the contemporary obsession with absolute originality seems strange to me. No one goes through a scientific article, sentence by sentence, trying to find out whether each formulation has already appeared at some point in history. Citations are not proof of absolute originality; they are a limited way of recognizing relevant antecedents. Bach’s work is not worth less because it belongs to a tradition. It can only be understood because it belongs to a tradition.

This text is the second of a family of 9 autonomous texts extracted from the essay “Producing AI”, by Paulo Volker.

item.title: There Is No Alien in the Human Cultural Cauldron
item.author: pvolker@mdh-hability.com (Pvolker / Projeto Centauro)
item.description:
There Is No Alien in the Human Cultural Cauldron

I am an author. I have been writing systematically since I was fifteen. Perhaps that is why the way many professional authors and musicians have reacted to artificial intelligence in culture bothers me so much. It doesn’t bother me that they defend fair compensation, credit, transparency, or working conditions. Those are necessary issues. What bothers me is something else: the idea that books, music, and images produced with AI would be a foreign invasion, a kind of non-human force that arrived to corrupt a hitherto genuinely human culture.

AI may be, perhaps, one of the most human works we have ever produced. Not because it is a person, nor because it feels, suffers, or has a biography. But because it is capable of speaking, with knowledge of cause and fact, about an immense expanse of what humanity has recorded about itself. It is made of human language, human memory, human science, human art, human technique, human institutions, human errors, human imagination. And, more than that, it opens the possibility for a much larger portion of humanity to access this heritage and work upon it.

But they claim that something “made by AI” is not human. There is something profoundly mistaken in this position. It presupposes that an ontological frontier exists between the human and what humanity has built. As if an instrument could cease to be human simply because it is powerful. The axe does not cease to be human because it cuts more than the hand. The telescope does not cease to be human because it sees farther than the eye. AI does not cease to be human because it reorganizes more culture than an isolated individual could.

The resistance to AI in culture reveals, at bottom, a certain image of what it means to be human: the image of the solitary, self-sufficient creator who pulls works out of himself like drawing water from an original spring. This image has always been a fiction. The difference is that now we have an instrument that makes this fiction untenable. And that is why the reaction is so intense. It is not only about defending a market or working conditions. It is about defending an identity.

What is at stake is not whether AI can or cannot create. What is at stake is whether we accept that creation has always been, and continues to be, a collective, ancestral, technical, and accumulative process. Whether we accept that the author is not the origin of the cultural stock, but a point of passage. Whether we accept that there is no alien in the human cultural cauldron — only humans doing what they have always done: reorganizing the heritage they received.
